claims.text: FeCoNiCrAl deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock produces a sub-target coating thickness with minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
Changing the feedstock from 15–45 μm to predominantly 45–100 μm particles will increase deposition efficiency.
Changing to predominantly 45–100 μm particles will increase net coating thickness.
The coarser feedstock will preserve coating integrity.
The coarser feedstock will minimize in-flight oxidation relative to the 15–45 μm baseline.
Larger feedstock particles produce thicker, well-flattened splats.
Larger particles have a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio.
A lower relative particle surface area reduces susceptibility to in-flight oxidation.
Coarser particles have higher thermal inertia.
The higher thermal inertia of coarser particles allows them to retain heat and melt more fully during flight.
More complete melting increases splat flattening and interlamellar bonding.
Improved splat flattening and interlamellar bonding will produce a thicker, adherent coating without significant oxidation.
The coarser-feedstock coating will retain phase makeup comparable to the 15–45 μm-feedstock coating.
The intervention can remain effective when deposited by atmospheric plasma spraying under low oxygen partial pressure with similar substrate preparation.
The resulting bond coat can perform under aero-engine thermal-barrier-coating service conditions up to 1000–1100 °C.
Excessively large particles can impair splat flattening.
Spray-parameter optimization may be necessary to obtain sufficient melting and avoid defects when using larger particles.

contradictions.description: The intervention calls for marginal adjustment of feed rate and spray distance to accommodate larger particles, whereas the controlled experiment specifies identical conditions except for particle size and explicitly maintains the same spray distance and power. Thus, the experiment does not directly test the intervention as formulated.

The mechanism states that higher thermal inertia makes larger particles melt more fully, while the uncertainty field acknowledges that sufficient melting of the larger particles may be difficult to achieve. This is an unresolved tension in the proposed causal mechanism.
